questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: ``The hold of the nationalist imagination on our colonial past is such that anything inadequately or improperly nationalist is just not history.'' Which of the following statements best reflects the author's opinion?
options: History is viewed through the filter of nationalism.
Nationalism has to be both adequately and properly imagined.
questions.explanation:
The author states that nationalism's hold on the colonial past is so strong that anything inadequately or improperly imagined ``is just not history.'' This implies history itself is viewed and filtered through the lens of nationalism — not that nationalism is good or bad, but that it acts as the medium through which the colonial past is perceived.
  • A. ``Nationalists are highly imaginative'' — not stated; imagination here refers to a collective construct, not a personal skill. Incorrect.
  • B. ``History is viewed through the filter of nationalism'' — directly supported: only nationalism-consistent narratives qualify as history. Correct.
  • C. ``Our colonial past never happened'' — not implied anywhere. Incorrect.
  • D. ``Nationalism must be adequately and properly imagined'' — this is a prescription not present in the passage. Incorrect.
\[\boxed{\text{B) History is viewed through the filter of nationalism.}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Arun, Gulab, Neel and Shweta must choose one shirt each from a pile of four shirts coloured red, pink, blue and white respectively. Arun dislikes the colour red and Shweta dislikes the colour white. Gulab and Neel like all the colours. In how many different ways can they choose the shirts so that no one has a shirt with a colour he or she dislikes?
questions.explanation:
4 people (Arun, Gulab, Neel, Shweta) each choose 1 shirt from piles of red, pink, blue, white (4 shirts each colour). Constraints:
  • Arun dislikes red.
  • Shweta dislikes white.
  • Gulab and Neel like all colours.
Count ways so that no colour appears more than once (each person gets a different colour): Total permutations of 4 colours to 4 people \(= 4! = 24\). Subtract: Arun gets red OR Shweta gets white (by inclusion-exclusion): Arun gets red: remaining \(3! = 6\) ways. Shweta gets white: remaining \(3! = 6\) ways. Both (Arun=red, Shweta=white): \(2! = 2\) ways. Invalid \(= 6 + 6 - 2 = 10\). \[\text{Valid} = 24 - 10 = 14\] \[\boxed{\text{D) 14}}\]
Key points
  • Treat as permutation with forbidden positions; apply inclusion-exclusion.
  • Total \(-\) (Arun=red) \(-\) (Shweta=white) \(+\) (both forbidden simultaneously).

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Choose the option with words that are not synonyms.
questions.explanation:
Find the pair that are NOT synonyms.
  • A. aversion, dislike — synonyms
  • B. luminous, radiant — synonyms
  • C. plunder, loot — synonyms
  • D. yielding, resistant — antonyms
\[\boxed{\text{D) yielding, resistant}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Saturn is to be seen on a clear night with the naked eye.
questions.explanation:
``Saturn is to be seen on a clear night with the naked eye.'' ``Bright enough'' is the correct phrase (adjective + enough). \[\boxed{\text{B) bright enough}}\]
Key points
  • ``Enough'' follows adjectives: ``bright enough,'' ``tall enough.''
  • ``Enough bright'' is grammatically incorrect in standard English.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: There are five buildings called V, W, X, Y and Z in a row (not necessarily in that order). V is to the West of W. Z is to the East of X and the West of V. W is to the West of Y. Which is the building in the middle?
questions.explanation:
Analyze the spatial constraints sequentially from West to East:
  • From "\(Z\) is to the East of \(X\) and the West of \(V\)": \(X \longrightarrow Z \longrightarrow V\)
  • From "\(V\) is to the West of \(W\)" and "\(W\) is to the West of \(Y\)": \(V \longrightarrow W \longrightarrow Y\)
Combining these relative positions gives the unique linear sequence: \[\text{(West)} \quad X \longrightarrow Z \longrightarrow \mathbf{V} \longrightarrow W \longrightarrow Y \quad \text{(East)}\] The building exactly in the middle position is V. \[\boxed{\text {A) V}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: A test has twenty questions worth 100 marks in total. There are two types of questions. Multiple choice questions are worth 3 marks each and essay questions are worth 11 marks each. How many multiple choice questions does the exam have?
questions.explanation: 20 questions, 100 marks total. MCQ worth 3 marks, essay worth 11 marks. Let \(x\) = MCQ count, \(y\) = essay count. \[x + y = 20, \quad 3x + 11y = 100\] \[3(20 - y) + 11y = 100 \implies 60 + 8y = 100 \implies y = 5,\quad x = 15\] \[\boxed{\text{B) 15}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: ``We lived in a culture that denied any merit to literary works, considering them important only when they were handmaidens to something seemingly more urgent -- namely ideology. This was a country where all gestures, even the most private, were interpreted in political terms.'' The author's belief that ideology is not as important as literature is revealed by the word:
questions.explanation:
The author states literary works were considered important only when they were ``handmaidens'' to ideology — implying ideology's dominance was not absolute but merely an appearance. The word `seemingly' reveals the author's belief: ideology's urgency was not genuine but only apparent, suggesting literature is in fact more important than ideology pretends to be.
  • `culture' — describes the setting, no judgment implied. Incorrect.
  • `seemingly' — signals the author's scepticism; ideology only appeared more urgent, not truly so. Correct.
  • `urgent' — describes ideology's claimed priority, not the author's doubt of it. Incorrect.
  • `political' — neutral descriptor, no comparative judgment. Incorrect.
\[\boxed{\text{B) `seemingly'}}\]
Key points
  • ``Seemingly'' = only on the surface; the author uses it to undercut ideology's claimed superiority.
  • The question asks which word reveals the author's belief — look for the word that carries implicit doubt or irony.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: There are three boxes. One contains apples, another contains oranges and the last one contains both apples and oranges. All three are known to be incorrectly labelled. If you are permitted to open just one box and then pull out and inspect only one fruit, which box would you open to determine the contents of all three boxes?
questions.explanation:
To solve this puzzle, we must utilize the critical piece of information given: all three boxes are incorrectly labelled. 1. Identify the Labels and Possible Contents
The three available labels on the boxes are:
  • `Apples'
  • `Oranges'
  • `Apples and Oranges'
2. Analyze the Strategy of Opening the `Apples and Oranges' Box
Since the box labelled `Apples and Oranges' is definitely mislabelled, it cannot contain a mixture of both fruits. Therefore, it must contain only apples or only oranges. Let's pick a fruit from this box to determine its true contents:
  • Case I: The picked fruit is an Apple.
    • The box labelled `Apples and Oranges' actually contains Apples.
    • We are left with two unverified boxes labelled `Apples' and `Oranges'.
    • Since the box labelled `Oranges' cannot contain oranges (due to mislabelling) and the apples are already accounted for, it must contain the remaining mixture: Apples and Oranges.
    • Consequently, the box labelled `Apples' must contain Oranges.
  • Case II: The picked fruit is an Orange.
    • The box labelled `Apples and Oranges' actually contains Oranges.
    • By applying the same elimination logic, the box labelled `Apples' must contain the mixture Apples and Oranges.
    • Consequently, the box labelled `Oranges' must contain Apples.
In both cases, inspecting a single fruit from the box labelled `Apples and Oranges' completely reveals the contents of all three boxes. \[\boxed{\text{B) The box labelled ‘Apples and Oranges’}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: with someone else's email account is now a very serious offence.
questions.explanation:
`` with someone else's email account is now a very serious offence.'' ``Tampering'' = interfering with something without authorisation — fits email account misuse perfectly. \[\boxed{\text{C) Tampering}}\]
Key points
  • ``Tamper with'' = to interfere or meddle with something, especially without permission.
  • ``Involving'' and ``assisting'' do not collocate with ``with someone's account'' in this legal sense.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question:
Consider the following sentences: All benches are beds. No bed is a bulb. Some bulbs are lamps. Which of the following can be inferred?
  1. Some beds are lamps.
  2. Some lamps are beds.
questions.explanation:
Premises: All benches are beds. No bed is a bulb. Some bulbs are lamps.
  • i. Some beds are lamps: Beds \(\cap\) bulbs \(= \emptyset\) (no bed is a bulb). Lamps are subset of bulbs. So beds \(\cap\) lamps \(= \emptyset\). False.
  • ii. Some lamps are beds: same reasoning — False.
Both i and ii are false. \[\boxed{\text{D) Neither i nor ii}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: The old concert hall was demolished because of fears that the foundation would be affected by the construction of the new metro line in the area. Modern technology for underground metro construction tried to mitigate the impact of pressurized air pockets created by the excavation of large amounts of soil. But even with these safeguards, it was feared that the soil below the concert hall would not be stable. From this, one can infer that
options: the foundations of old buildings create pressurized air pockets underground, which are difficult to handle during metro construction.
metro construction has to be done carefully considering its impact on the foundations of existing buildings.
old buildings in an area form an impossible hurdle to metro construction in that area.
pressurized air can be used to excavate large amounts of soil from underground areas.
questions.explanation:
The passage states the concert hall would be demolished due to fears about foundation stability during metro construction. The pressurized air pockets and large soil excavation were mitigated by modern technology, but the soil below was still feared unstable. The inference is: \[\boxed{\text{B) metro construction has to be done carefully considering its impact on the foundations of existing buildings.}}\]
Key points
  • The passage focuses on the risk metro construction poses to existing structures.
  • Option B is the most direct and accurate inference from the given context.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: The event would have been successful if you _____ able to come.
questions.explanation: ``The event would have been successful if you able to come.'' Third conditional (unreal past): ``would have been'' in main clause requires ``had been'' in if-clause. \[\boxed{\text{B) had been}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: There was no doubt that their work was <u>thorough</u>. Which of the words below is closest in meaning to the underlined word above?
questions.explanation:
``There was no doubt that their work was thorough.'' Underlined word: thorough. ``Thorough'' = complete, exhaustive, done with great care. \[\boxed{\text{B) complete}}\]
Key points
  • ``Thorough'' = carried out fully and carefully; closest synonym is ``complete.''
  • ``Sloppy'' is an antonym; ``pretty'' and ``haphazard'' are unrelated.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Four cards lie on a table. Each card has a number printed on one side and a colour on the other. The faces visible on the cards are 2, 3, red, and blue. Proposition: If a card has an even value on one side, then its opposite face is red. The cards which MUST be turned over to verify the above proposition are
questions.explanation:
4 cards: numbers 2, 3, red, blue on sides. Proposition: even number on one side \(\Rightarrow\) red on other side. To falsify: find a card with even number on one side and non-red (blue) on other. Cards to turn:
  • ``2'' (even) — must check other side is red.
  • ``red'' — if other side is odd, no problem; if even, must be red (already is). Not needed.
  • ``3'' (odd) — proposition doesn't apply. Skip.
  • ``blue'' — if other side is even, proposition violated. Must check.
Cards to turn: 2 and blue. \[\boxed{\text{C) 2, blue}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Bhaichung was observing the pattern of people entering and leaving a car service centre. There was a single window where customers were being served. He saw that people inevitably came out of the centre in the order that they went in. However, the time they spent inside seemed to vary a lot: some people came out in a matter of minutes while for others it took much longer. From this, what can one conclude?
options: The centre operates on a first-come-first-served basis, but with variable service times depending on specific customer needs.
Customers were served in an arbitrary order, since they took varying amounts of time for service completion in the centre.
Since some people came out within a few minutes of entering the centre, the system is likely to operate on a last-come-first-served basis.
Entering the centre early ensured that one would have shorter service times and most people attempted to do this.
questions.explanation:
We need to identify the logical conclusion about the service center's operational queue system based on Bhaichung's observations. 1. Analyze the Core Observations
Let us break down the two factual observations given in the problem statement:
  • Observation 1: "People inevitably came out of the centre in the order that they went in."
    • This means the order of exit matches the order of entry exactly.
    • In data structures and queuing theory, an orderly exit corresponding strictly to entry order defines a First-In, First-Out (FIFO) or First-Come, First-Served (FCFS) model.
  • Observation 2: "The time they spent inside seemed to vary a lot."
    • This directly implies that the processing or service time varies on a per-customer basis, depending on their individual requirements.
2. Evaluate the Choices
  • Option A: Perfectly matches both observations (First-Come-First-Served basis with variable service times) .
  • Option B: Contradicts Observation 1 by suggesting an "arbitrary order" .
  • Option C: Suggests a "last-come-first-served" (LIFO) model, which contradicts the entry-exit sequence .
  • Option D: Incorrectly claims that entering early ensures a shorter service time, which is false since service time depends on specific customer needs, not entry timestamps .
\[\boxed{\text {A) The centre operates on a first-come-first-served basis, but with variable service times depending on needs.}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question:
A map shows the elevations of Darjeeling, Gangtok, Kalimpong, Pelling, and Siliguri. Kalimpong is at a lower elevation than Gangtok. Pelling is at a lower elevation than Gangtok. Pelling is at a higher elevation than Siliguri. Darjeeling is at a higher elevation than Gangtok. Which of the following statements can be inferred from the paragraph above?
  1. Pelling is at a higher elevation than Kalimpong
  2. Kalimpong is at a lower elevation than Darjeeling
  3. Kalimpong is at a lower elevation than Pelling
  4. Siliguri is at a lower elevation than Gangtok
questions.explanation:
We establish the relative elevation relationships directly from the constraints :
  • \(\text{Darjeeling} > \text{Gangtok}\)
  • \(\text{Gangtok} > \text{Kalimpong}\)
  • \(\text{Gangtok} > \text{Pelling} > \text{Siliguri}\)
Combining these gives the partial vertical hierarchy: \[\text{Darjeeling} > \text{Gangtok} > \begin{cases} \text{Kalimpong} \\ \text{Pelling} > \text{Siliguri} \end{cases}\] Evaluate Statements:
  • ii. True: Since \(\text{Darjeeling} > \text{Gangtok} > \text{Kalimpong}\).
  • iv. True: Since \(\text{Gangtok} > \text{Pelling} > \text{Siliguri}\).
Statements i and iii are undetermined because there is no direct path comparing Kalimpong and Pelling. Thus, only ii and iv can be inferred. \[\boxed{\text {C) Only ii and iv }}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: P, Q, R, S, T and U are seated around a circular table. R is seated two places to the right of Q. P is seated three places to the left of R. S is seated opposite U. If P and U now switch seats, which of the following must necessarily be true?
options: P is immediately to the right of R
T is immediately to the left of P
T is immediately to the left of P or P is immediately to the right of Q
U is immediately to the right of R or P is immediately to the left of T
questions.explanation:
Based on the initial constraints given in the problem statement, we map out the relative positions around the circular table:
  • \(R\) is seated two places to the right of \(Q\).
  • \(P\) is seated three places to the left of \(R\) (which means \(P\) and \(R\) are diametrically opposite each other in a 6-seat arrangement).
  • \(S\) is seated opposite \(U\).
From these conditions, two valid initial arrangements can be constructed depending on where the remaining seats are filled:
  • Possibility 1 (Clockwise order): \(T \rightarrow R \rightarrow S \rightarrow Q \rightarrow P \rightarrow U\)
  • Possibility 2 (Clockwise order): \(T \rightarrow R \rightarrow U \rightarrow Q \rightarrow P \rightarrow S\)
The problem states that \(P\) and \(U\) switch seats. Let us update both configurations:
  • Modified Possibility 1: \(T \rightarrow R \rightarrow S \rightarrow Q \rightarrow U \rightarrow P\)
  • Modified Possibility 2: \(T \rightarrow R \rightarrow P \rightarrow Q \rightarrow U \rightarrow S\)
\[\boxed{\text {C) T is immediately to the left of P or P is immediately to the right of Q }}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: He was one of my best and I felt his loss .
questions.explanation:
The sentence requires two blanks: a plural noun after ``best'' and an adverb modifying ``felt his loss''.
  • A. friend, keenly — friend is singular; ``one of my best friend'' is ungrammatical.
  • B. friends, keen — keen is an adjective, not an adverb; cannot modify felt.
  • C. friend, keener — singular friend and comparative keener both incorrect.
  • D. friends, keenly — friends is plural (); keenly is the correct adverb to modify felt his loss. \(\checkmark\)
\[\boxed{\text{D) friends, keenly}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: A right-angled cone (with base radius 5 cm and height 12 cm), as shown in the figure below, is rolled on the ground keeping the point P fixed until the point Q (at the base of the cone, as shown) touches the ground again. By what angle (in radians) does the cone travel?

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: In a company with 100 employees, 45 earn Rs.~20,000 per month, 25 earn Rs.~30,000, 20 earn Rs.~40,000, 8 earn Rs.~60,000, and 2 earn Rs.~1,50,000. The median of the salaries is
questions.explanation:
Total employees \(= 100\). Compute the total salary bill: \[\text{Total} = 45(20{,}000) + 25(30{,}000) + 20(40{,}000) + 8(60{,}000) + 2(1{,}50{,}000)\] \[= 9{,}00{,}000 + 7{,}50{,}000 + 8{,}00{,}000 + 4{,}80{,}000 + 3{,}00{,}000 = 32{,}30{,}000\] Median salary: with 100 employees, the median is the average of the 50th and 51st values. Cumulative counts: \[45\ (\leq 20{,}000),\quad 45+25=70\ (\leq 30{,}000)\] Both the 50th and 51st employees fall in the Rs.,30,000 group. \[\text{Median} = \text{Rs.}\;30{,}000\] \[\boxed{\text{B) Rs.\;30{,}000}}\]
Key points
  • Median for \(n\) (even) values \(=\) average of \(\left(\tfrac{n}{2}\right)\)th and \(\left(\tfrac{n}{2}+1\right)\)th values.
  • Use cumulative frequency to locate which salary group contains the median position.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: P, Q, and R talk about S's car collection. P states that S has at least 3 cars. Q believes that S has less than 3 cars. R indicates that to his knowledge, S has at least one car. Only one of P, Q and R is right. The number of cars owned by S is
questions.explanation:
Statements made by P, Q, and R about S's car collection:
  • P: S has at least 3 cars \(\Rightarrow S \geq 3\).
  • Q: S has less than 3 cars \(\Rightarrow S < 3\).
  • R: S has at least 1 car \(\Rightarrow S \geq 1\).
Only one of P, Q, R is right. Case: Q is right (\(S < 3\), i.e. \(S \leq 2\)):
  • P says \(S \geq 3\) — False.
  • R says \(S \geq 1\) — True if \(S \geq 1\).
This gives two true statements unless \(S = 0\), but \(S = 0\) makes R false too, leaving only Q true. Case: \(S = 0\):
P false, Q true (\(0 < 3\)), R false (\(0 < 1\)) — exactly one true. \[S = 0 \implies \text{Number of cars owned by S} = 0\] \[\boxed{\text{A)}\;0}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question:
What is the sum of the missing digits in the subtraction problem below?
5____
\(-\)48_89
1111
questions.explanation:
Two possible cases exist for the missing digits: Case 1:
\[\begin{array}{r} 5\;0\;1\;0\;0 \\ -\;4\;8\;9\;8\;9 \\ \hline 0\;1\;1\;1\;1 \end{array}\] \[\text{Sum} = 1 + 9 = 10\] Case 2:
\[\begin{array}{r} 5\;0\;0\;0\;0 \\ -\;4\;8\;8\;8\;9 \\ \hline 0\;1\;1\;1\;1 \end{array}\] \[\text{Sum} = 0 + 8 = 8\] Since two different sums (8 and 10) are both valid, the answer cannot be uniquely determined. \[\boxed{\text{D) Cannot be determined}}\]
Key points
  • Check all valid digit combinations that satisfy the subtraction column by column.
  • If more than one solution exists, the answer is ``Cannot be determined.''

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Let \(S_1\) be the plane figure consisting of the points \((x, y)\) given by the inequalities \(|x - 1| \leq 2\) and \(|y + 2| \leq 3\). Let \(S_2\) be the plane figure given by the inequalities \(x - y \geq -2\), \(y \geq 1\), and \(x \leq 3\). Let \(S\) be the union of \(S_1\) and \(S_2\). The area of \(S\) is

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question:
The growth of bacteria (lactobacillus) in milk leads to curd formation. A minimum bacterial population density of 0.8 (in suitable units) is needed to form curd. In the graph below, the population density of lactobacillus in 1 litre of milk is plotted as a function of time, at two different temperatures, \(25\,^\circ\)C and \(37\,^\circ\)C. Consider the following statements based on the data shown above:
  1. The growth in bacterial population stops earlier at \(37\,^\circ\)C as compared to \(25\,^\circ\)C
  2. The time taken for curd formation at \(25\,^\circ\)C is twice the time taken at \(37\,^\circ\)C
Which one of the following options is correct?
questions.explanation:
From the graph, two statements are evaluated: Statement i: The growth in bacterial population stops earlier at \(37\,^{\circ}\text{C}\) compared to \(25\,^{\circ}\text{C}\). From the graph, the \(37\,^{\circ}\text{C}\) curve reaches saturation (population density \(\approx 1.0\)) at an earlier time than the \(25\,^{\circ}\text{C}\) curve. Statement i is True. Statement ii: The time taken for curd formation at \(25\,^{\circ}\text{C}\) is twice the time taken at \(37\,^{\circ}\text{C}\). Curd forms at population density \(= 0.8\). From the graph: \[t_{37} \approx 80\,\text{min}, \quad t_{25} \approx 120\,\text{min}\] \[\frac{t_{25}}{t_{37}} = \frac{120}{80} = 1.5 \neq 2\] Statement ii is False. Only statement i is correct as directly visible from the graph. \[\boxed{\text{A) Only i}}\]
Key points
  • Higher temperature (\(37\,^{\circ}\text{C}\)) accelerates bacterial growth \(\Rightarrow\) saturation reached earlier.
  • Read curd-formation time at density \(= 0.8\) for both curves to verify statement ii.
  • \(t_{25}/t_{37} \approx 1.5\), not 2 — statement ii fails.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: If \(a\) and \(b\) are integers and \(a - b\) is even, which of the following must always be even?
questions.explanation: \(a - b\) is even \(\Rightarrow\) \(a\) and \(b\) have the same parity. Check \(ab - b = b(a-1)\): \[\text{Both odd: } b(a-1) = \text{odd} \times \text{even} = \text{even}\ \checkmark\] \[\text{Both even: } b(a-1) = \text{even} \times \text{odd} = \text{even}\ \checkmark\] \[\boxed{\text{D) } ab - b}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: A couple has 2 children. The probability that both children are boys if the older one is a boy is
questions.explanation: Older child is a boy. Restricted sample space: \(\{BB, BG\}\). \[P(\text{both boys} \mid \text{older is boy}) = \frac{1}{2}\] \[\boxed{\text{C) } \frac{1}{2}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: P looks at Q while Q looks at R. P is married, R is not. The number of pairs of people in which a married person is looking at an unmarried person is
questions.explanation:
P (married) \(\to\) Q \(\to\) R (unmarried). If Q is married: Q(married) \(\to\) R(unmarried) \(= 1\) valid pair. If Q is unmarried: P(married) \(\to\) Q(unmarried) \(= 1\) valid pair. \[\boxed{\text{B) 2}}\]
Key points
  • Enumerate Q's marital status systematically.
  • Both directed pairs \((P \to Q)\) and \((Q \to R)\) are candidates depending on Q's status.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: X bullocks and Y tractors take 8 days to plough a field. If we halve the number of bullocks and double the number of tractors, it takes 5 days to plough the same field. How many days will it take X bullocks alone to plough the field?
questions.explanation:
Let bullock rate \(= b\), tractor rate \(= t\). \[(Xb + Yt) \times 8 = \left(\frac{X}{2}b + 2Yt\right) \times 5\] \[8Xb + 8Yt = \frac{5X}{2}b + 10Yt
\implies \frac{11X}{2}b = 2Yt \implies \frac{Yt}{Xb} = \frac{11}{4}\] Time for \(X\) bullocks alone: \[T = \frac{8(Xb + Yt)}{Xb} = 8\left(1 + \frac{11}{4}\right) = 8 \times \frac{15}{4} = 30\,\text{days}\] \[\boxed{\text{A) 30 days}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: There are 4 women P, Q, R, S, and 5 men V, W, X, Y, Z in a group. We are required to form pairs each consisting of one woman and one man. P is not to be paired with Z, and Y must necessarily be paired with someone. In how many ways can 4 such pairs be formed?
questions.explanation: Total arrangements (choose 1 man to exclude from 5, assign rest to 4 women): \[5 \times 4! = 120\] Subtract cases where P is paired with Z: \[4 \times 3! = 24\] Subtract cases where Y is excluded: \[4! = 24\] Add back overlap (P-Z paired AND Y excluded): \[3! = 6\] \[\text{Valid} = 120 - 24 - 24 + 6 = 78\] \[\boxed{\text{C) 78}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question:
In the graph below, the concentration of a particular pollutant in a lake is plotted over (alternate) days of a month in winter (average temperature \(10\,^\circ\)C) and a month in summer (average temperature \(30\,^\circ\)C). Consider the following statements based on the data shown above:
  1. Over the given months, the difference between the maximum and the minimum pollutant concentrations is the same in both winter and summer.
  2. There are at least four days in the summer month such that the pollutant concentrations on those days are within 1 ppm of the pollutant concentrations on the corresponding days in the winter month.
Which one of the following options is correct?
questions.explanation:
Statement i: Winter range \(\approx 9 - 2 = 7\,\text{ppm}\); Summer range \(\approx 8 - 3 = 5\,\text{ppm}\). Not equal. False. Statement ii: From graph, curves are within \(1\,\text{ppm}\) on at least 4 days. True. \[\boxed{\text{B) Only ii}}\]
Key points
  • Read min and max values carefully from both curves.
  • Count days where \(|C_{\text{summer}} - C_{\text{winter}}| \leq 1\,\text{ppm}\).

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: In the summer, water consumption is known to decrease overall by 25%. A Water Board official states that in the summer household consumption decreases by 20%, while other consumption increases by 70%. Which of the following statements is correct?
options: The ratio of household to other consumption is 8/17
The ratio of household to other consumption is 1/17
The ratio of household to other consumption is 17/8
There are errors in the official's statement.
questions.explanation: Let household \(= H\), other \(= O\). Overall decrease \(= 25\%\): \[0.8H + 1.7O = 0.75(H + O)\] \[0.05H = -0.95O \implies \frac{H}{O} = -19\] Negative ratio is impossible \(\Rightarrow\) official's statement contains errors. \[\boxed{\text{D) There are errors in the official's statement}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: 40% of deaths on city roads may be attributed to drunken driving. The number of degrees needed to represent this as a slice of a pie chart is
questions.explanation:
Key Concept:
  • A complete pie chart represents \(100\%\).
  • The total central angle of a complete circle is \(360^\circ\).
  • Therefore, \(1\%\) of a pie chart corresponds to: \[\frac{360^\circ}{100} = 3.6^\circ\]
Step-by-step Calculation:
Given that the attributed cause accounts for \(40\%\) of the total circle, we multiply the percentage by the total degrees of a circle: \[\text{Sector Angle } (\theta) = \frac{\text{Given Percentage}}{100} \times 360^\circ\] \[\theta = \frac{40}{100} \times 360^\circ = 0.40 \times 360^\circ\] \[\theta = 144^\circ\] \[\boxed{\text{B) } 144}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Trucks (10 m long) and cars (5 m long) go on a single lane bridge. There must be a gap of at least 20 m after each truck and a gap of at least 15 m after each car. Trucks and cars travel at a speed of 36 km/h. If cars and trucks go alternately, what is the maximum number of vehicles that can use the bridge in one hour?
questions.explanation:
One repeating truck-car unit length: \[10 + 20 + 5 + 15 = 50\,\text{m}\] Distance in 1 hour at \(36\,\text{km/h} = 10\,\text{m/s}\): \[d = 10 \times 3600 = 36000\,\text{m}\] \[N_{\text{vehicles}} = \frac{36000}{50} \times 2 = 1440\] \[\boxed{\text{A) 1440}}\]
Key points
  • One unit = truck (\(10\,\text{m}\)) + gap (\(20\,\text{m}\)) + car (\(5\,\text{m}\)) + gap (\(15\,\text{m}\)) \(= 50\,\text{m}\).
  • Multiply units by 2 for total vehicle count.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: There are 3 Indians and 3 Chinese in a group of 6 people. How many subgroups of this group can we choose so that every subgroup has at least one Indian?
questions.explanation:
Total non-empty subgroups \(= 2^6 - 1 = 63\). Subgroups with no Indians (all Chinese only) \(= 2^3 - 1 = 7\). \[\text{Valid subgroups} = 63 - 7 = 56\] \[\boxed{\text{A) 56}}\]
Key points
  • Complementary counting: Total \(-\) all-Chinese subgroups.
  • \(2^n\) includes empty set; subtract 1 for non-empty constraint.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: A contour line joins locations having the same height above the mean sea level. The following is a contour plot of a geographical region. Contour lines are shown at 25 m intervals in this plot. The path from P to Q is best described by
questions.explanation:
Tracing path from P to Q on the contour plot :
  • P starts at \(\approx 550\,\text{m}\)
  • Then descends into valley \(\approx 500\,\text{m}\): Down.
  • Then rises toward Q at \(\approx 575\,\text{m}\): Up.
  • Then descends into valley \(\approx 550\,\text{m}\): Down.
\[\boxed{\text{C) Down-Up-Down}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: A rule states that in order to drink beer, one must be over 18 years old. In a bar, there are 4 people. P is 16 years old, Q is 25 years old, R is drinking milkshake and S is drinking a beer. What must be checked to ensure that the rule is being followed?
options: Only P's drink and S's age
Only P's drink, Q's drink and S's age
questions.explanation:
Rule: must be over 18 to drink beer. People: P (16), Q (25), R (drinking milkshake), S (drinking beer).
  • P (16) is underage \(\Rightarrow\) P's drink must be checked.
  • S is drinking beer \(\Rightarrow\) S's age must be checked to verify \(> 18\).

questions.question: Fatima starts from point P, goes North for 3 km, and then East for 4 km to reach point Q. She then turns to face point P and goes 15 km in that direction. She then goes North for 6 km. How far is she from point P, and in which direction should she go to reach point P?
questions.explanation: Set up coordinates with \(P\) at the origin \((0,0)\). Step 1: Fatima goes North \(3\,\text{km}\) then East \(4\,\text{km}\) to reach \(Q\): \[Q = (4, 3)\] Step 2: Distance \(PQ\): \[PQ = \sqrt{4^2 + 3^2} = \sqrt{16 + 9} = 5\,\text{km}\] Step 3: She turns to face \(P\) from \(Q\) and walks \(15\,\text{km}\). Unit vector from \(Q\) toward \(P\): \[\hat{u} = \frac{(0,0)-(4,3)}{5} = \left(\frac{-4}{5},\ \frac{-3}{5}\right)\] Position after \(15\,\text{km}\) toward \(P\): \[(4,3) + 15 \times \left(\frac{-4}{5},\ \frac{-3}{5}\right) = (4-12,\ 3-9) = (-8,\ -6)\] Step 4: She then goes North \(6\,\text{km}\): \[(-8,\ -6+6) = (-8,\ 0)\] Step 5: Distance from \(P(0,0)\): \[d = \sqrt{(-8)^2 + 0^2} = 8\,\text{km}\] Since her final position is \((-8, 0)\), i.e., \(8\,\text{km}\) due West of \(P\), she must travel East to reach \(P\). \[\boxed{\text{A: 8\,km, East}}\]

questions.question: 500 students are taking one or more courses out of Chemistry, Physics, and Mathematics. Registration records indicate course enrolment as follows: Chemistry (329), Physics (186), Mathematics (295), Chemistry and Physics (83), Chemistry and Mathematics (217), and Physics and Mathematics (63). How many students are taking all 3 subjects?
questions.explanation:
Use inclusion-exclusion. Let \(C = 329\), \(P = 186\), \(M = 295\), \(CP = 83\), \(CM = 217\), \(PM = 63\), total \(= 500\). \[C \cup P \cup M = C + P + M - CP - CM - PM + CPM\] \[500 = 329 + 186 + 295 - 83 - 217 - 63 + CPM\] \[500 = 447 + CPM \implies CPM = 500 - 447 = 53\] \[\boxed{\text{D) 53}}\]
Key points
  • Inclusion-exclusion: \(|A\cup B\cup C| = |A|+|B|+|C|-|A\cap B|-|B\cap C|-|A\cap C|+|A\cap B\cap C|\).

questions.question: 1200 men and 500 women can build a bridge in 2 weeks. 900 men and 250 women will take 3 weeks to build the same bridge. How many men will be needed to build the bridge in one week?
questions.explanation: Let work rate of 1 man \(= m\), 1 woman \(= w\). From condition 1: \(1200m + 500w\) complete bridge in \(2\) weeks. \[W = 2(1200m + 500w)\] From condition 2: \(900m + 250w\) complete in \(3\) weeks. \[W = 3(900m + 250w) = 2700m + 750w\] Equating: \[2400m + 1000w = 2700m + 750w\] \[250w = 300m \implies \frac{m}{w} = \frac{5}{6}\] Let \(m = 5k\), \(w = 6k\). Then: \[W = 2(1200 \times 5k + 500 \times 6k) = 2(6000k + 3000k) = 18000k\] For 1 week with \(N\) men (no women): \[N \times 5k \times 1 = 18000k \implies N = \frac{18000}{5} = 3600\] \[\boxed{\text{C) 3600}}\]

questions.question: Find the smallest number \(y\) such that \(y \times 162\) is a perfect cube.
questions.explanation: Find smallest \(y\) such that \(y \times 162\) is a perfect cube. \[162 = 2 \times 81 = 2 \times 3^4\] For a perfect cube, all prime factors need exponents divisible by 3: \[2^1 \times 3^4 \Rightarrow \text{need } 2^2 \times 3^2 = 4 \times 9 = 36\ \text{more... wait}\] \[2^1 \to \text{need } 2^2;\ 3^4 \to \text{need } 3^2 \Rightarrow y = 2^2 \times 3^2 = 4 \times 9 = 36\] Check: \(36 \times 162 = 5832 = 18^3\). \[\boxed{\text{D) 36}}\]

questions.question: The probability that a \(k\)-digit number does NOT contain the digits 0, 5, or 9 is
questions.explanation:
Probability that a \(k\)-digit number does NOT contain digits 0, 5, or 9. Each digit chosen from \(\{1,2,3,4,6,7,8\}\) (7 digits) out of 10 possible digits. \[P = \left(\frac{7}{10}\right)^k = 0.7^k\] \[\boxed{\text{C) } 0.7^k}\]
Key points
  • Each of the \(k\) digits independently avoids 3 forbidden digits \(\{0,5,9\}\).
  • Probability per digit \(= 7/10 = 0.7\); for \(k\) independent digits \(= 0.7^k\).
Mistakes to avoid
The first digit of a \(k\)-digit number cannot be 0 anyway, but since 0 is already excluded from valid digits, the formula \(0.7^k\) holds uniformly.

questions.question: Six people are seated around a circular table. There are at least two men and two women. There are at least three right-handed persons. Every woman has a left-handed person to her immediate right. None of the women are right-handed. The number of women at the table is
questions.explanation:
6 people seated around a circular table. Key constraints:
  • At least 2 men and 2 women.
  • At least 3 right-handed persons.
  • Every woman has a left-handed person to her immediate right.
  • No woman is right-handed (all women are left-handed).
Since all women are left-handed, the 3 right-handed persons must all be men \(\Rightarrow\) at least 3 right-handed men. With 6 seats and at least 3 right-handed men occupying 3 seats, only 3 seats remain. The 2 women must sit adjacently. Each woman needs a left-handed person to her immediate right: \[L^{(w)} \to L^{(w)} \to \underbrace{?}_{\text{left-handed man}}\] The seat immediately to the right of the second woman must be a left-handed man. This uses up the one remaining non-right-handed seat. Final arrangement:
\[R^{(m)},\ R^{(m)},\ R^{(m)},\ L^{(m)},\ L^{(w)},\ L^{(w)}\] Here \(R^{(m)}\) = right-handed man, \(L^{(m)}\) = left-handed man, \(L^{(w)}\) = left-handed woman. Total women \(= 2\), satisfying all constraints:
  • At least 2 men (4 men)
  • At least 2 women (2 women)
  • At least 3 right-handed (\(3 \times R^{(m)}\))
  • Each woman has left-handed person to her right
\[\boxed{\text{A) }2}\]
Key points
  • All women are left-handed \(\Rightarrow\) right-handed quota filled entirely by men.
  • 3 right-handed men \(+\) 1 left-handed man \(+\) 2 left-handed women \(= 6\) seats exactly.
  • The two women must sit together with a left-handed man immediately to their right.

questions.question: An air pressure contour line joins locations in a region having the same atmospheric pressure. The following is an air pressure contour plot of a geographical region. Contour lines are shown at 0.05 bar intervals in this plot. If the possibility of a thunderstorm is given by how fast air pressure rises or drops over a region, which of the following regions is most likely to have a thunderstorm?
questions.explanation:
The question defines the possibility of a thunderstorm by how fast air pressure rises or drops over a region. In a geographical contour map, this rate of change is represented by the spatial gradient of the contours. 1. Concept of Contour Gradients
  • Closely Spaced Contour Lines: Represent a rapid change in the variable (high gradient) over a short geographical distance.
  • Widely Spaced Contour Lines: Represent a gradual change in the variable (low gradient) over a longer geographical distance.
Therefore, the region with the highest density of contour lines will experience the fastest pressure rise or drop, making it the most likely location for a thunderstorm. 2. Evaluating Regions on the Map: Let us inspect the contour line density inside each designated circular area:
  • Region P: Located near a local peak, but the concentric rings are spaced moderately apart.
  • Region Q: Situated in a flat plain area where the contour lines are extremely sparse and wide apart, indicating a nearly constant pressure.
  • Region R: Positioned in the upper-left area where multiple closely nested contour lines (\(0.65\), \(0.7\), etc.) are packed tightly together. This extreme closeness indicates a steep steep pressure drop or rise over a short distance.
  • Region S: Encloses a local plateau/peak with relatively broad intervals between its innermost contours.
Since the contour lines are packed most densely in Region R, it has the highest pressure gradient. \[\boxed{\text{ C) R}}\]

questions.question: If the radius of a right circular cone is increased by 50%, its volume increases by
questions.explanation:
Radius of right circular cone increased by 50%: \(r' = 1.5r\). Height unchanged. Volume \(\propto r^2 h\): \[\frac{V'}{V} = \frac{(1.5r)^2 h}{r^2 h} = 2.25\] \[\text{Increase} = (2.25 - 1) \times 100\% = 125\%\] \[\boxed{\text{C) 125\%}}\]
Key points
  • \(V = \tfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h\); volume scales as \(r^2\) when \(h\) is fixed.
  • \((1.5)^2 = 2.25 \Rightarrow 125\%\) increase.

questions.question: The following sequence of numbers is arranged in increasing order: 1, \(x\), \(x\), \(x\), \(y\), \(y\), 9, 16, 18. Given that the mean and median are equal, and are also equal to twice the mode, the value of \(y\) is
questions.explanation:
From the ordered sequence of 9 terms: \(1, x, x, x, y, y, 9, 16, 18\):
  • \(\text{Mode} = x\) (appears 3 times)
  • \(\text{Median} = y\) (the 5th middle term)
Given the condition \(\text{Mean} = \text{Median} = 2 \times \text{Mode}\): \[y = 2x \implies x = \frac{y}{2}\] Set up the equation for the Mean: \[\frac{1 + 3x + 2y + 9 + 16 + 18}{9} = y\] \[44 + 3x + 2y = 9y \implies 7y - 3x = 44\] Substitute \(x = \dfrac{y}{2}\) into the linear system: \[7y - 3\left(\frac{y}{2}\right) = 44 \implies 11y = 88 \implies y = 8\] \[\boxed{ \text {D) 8}}\]

Students applying for hostel rooms are allotted rooms in order of seniority. Students already staying in a room will move if they get a room in their preferred list. Preferences of lower ranked applicants are ignored during allocation. Given the data below, which room will Ajit stay in?
NamesStudent seniorityCurrent roomRoom preference list

  • Room P: Amar \(\bullet\) Room Q: Anthony \(\bullet\) Room S: Ajit \(\bullet\) Room R: Vacant

questions.explanation:
Find last digit of \((2171)^7 + (2172)^9 + (2173)^{11} + (2174)^{13}\). Last digits of bases: 1, 2, 3, 4. \[1^{\text{any}} \to 1\] \[2^9: \text{cycle } 2,4,8,6 \text{ (period 4)};\ 9 \mod 4 = 1 \to 2\] \[3^{11}: \text{cycle } 3,9,7,1 \text{ (period 4)};\ 11 \mod 4 = 3 \to 7\] \[4^{13}: \text{cycle } 4,6 \text{ (period 2)};\ 13 \mod 2 = 1 \to 4\] \[\text{Sum of last digits} = 1 + 2 + 7 + 4 = 14 \to \text{last digit} = 4\] \[\boxed{\text{B) 4}}\]
Key points
  • Last digit of a power depends only on the last digit of the base and the exponent's remainder in the cycle.
  • Cycles: \(1^n\to1\); \(2^n\) period 4; \(3^n\) period 4; \(4^n\) period 2.

questions.question:
The bar graph below shows the output of five carpenters over one month, each of whom made different items of furniture: chairs, tables, and beds. Consider the following statements:
  1. The number of beds made by carpenter C2 is exactly the same as the number of tables made by carpenter C3.
  2. The total number of chairs made by all carpenters is less than the total number of tables.
Which one of the following is true?
questions.explanation:
We need to evaluate the truth value of two statements using the provided stacked bar graph. 1. Evaluate Statement (i):
"The number of beds made by carpenter C2 is exactly the same as the number of tables made by carpenter C3."
  • Beds by C2: Looking at the top segments (Bed), C2 spans from height \(12\) to \(20\). \[\text{Beds (C2)} = 20 - 12 = 8 \text{ units}\]
  • Tables by C3: Looking at the middle segments (Table), C3 spans from height \(5\) to \(13\). \[\text{Tables (C3)} = 13 - 5 = 8 \text{ units}\]
Since \(8 = 8\), Statement (i) is TRUE 2. Evaluate Statement (ii):
"The total number of chairs made by all carpenters is less than the total number of tables." Let us read the base height value for Chairs and the interval size for Tables across all carpenters:
  • Total Chairs (Base segments):
    \[\text{Chairs} = 2 \text{ (C1)} + 10 \text{ (C2)} + 5 \text{ (C3)} + 2 \text{ (C4)} + 4 \text{ (C5)} = 23\]
  • Total Tables (Middle segments):
    \[\text{Tables} = (9-2) + (12-10) + (13-5) + (5-2) + (14-4)\] \[\text{Tables} = 7 + 2 + 8 + 3 + 10 = 30\]
Since \(23 < 30\), Statement (ii) is TRUE Because both statements are correct, the choice matches option C \[\boxed{\text {C) Both i and ii}}\]

questions.question: What is the value of \(x\) when \(81 \times \left(\dfrac{16}{25}\right)^{x+2} \div \left(\dfrac{2}{5}\right)^{2x+4} = 144\),?
questions.explanation:
We solve the given exponential equation by breaking it down into prime bases (\(2\), \(3\), and \(5\)): \[81 \times \left(\frac{16}{25}\right)^{x+2} \div \left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^{2x+4} = 144\] 1. Prime Factoring the Components
\[81 = 3^4, \quad 144 = 2^4 \times 3^2, \quad \frac{16}{25} = \frac{2^4}{5^2}\] 2. Expanding the Left-Hand Side (LHS)
Substitute the prime bases into the expression: \[3^4 \times \frac{2^{4x+8}}{5^{2x+4}} \times \frac{5^{2x+4}}{3^{2x+4}} = 2^4 \times 3^2\] 3. Canceling and Simplifying
The base \(5\) terms cancel out completely, leaving: \[3^{4 - (2x+4)} \times 2^{4x+8} = 2^4 \times 3^2\] \[3^{-2x} \times 2^{4x+8} = 3^2 \times 2^4\] 4. Comparing Exponents
Equating the powers of base \(3\): \[-2x = 2 \implies x = -1\] *(Verification using base \(2\): \(4x + 8 = 4 \implies 4x = -4 \implies x = -1\).)* \[\boxed{ \text{ B) -1}}\]

Two dice thrown. Probability that product of top faces is a perfect square. Perfect square products from two dice (1--6): 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36. Favourable pairs \((a,b)\) where \(ab\) is perfect square:
  • \(ab=1\): \((1,1)\) — 1 way
  • \(ab=4\): \((1,4),(4,1),(2,2)\) — 3 ways
  • \(ab=9\): \((3,3)\) — 1 way
  • \(ab=16\): \((4,4),(2,8)\times,(8,2)\times\) — only \((4,4)\) — 1 way
  • \(ab=25\): \((5,5)\) — 1 way
  • \(ab=36\): \((6,6)\) — 1 way
Total favourable \(= 1+3+1+1+1+1 = 8\) \[P = \frac{8}{36} = \frac{2}{9}\] \[\boxed{\text{B) 2/9}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Budhan covers a distance of 19 km in 2 hours by cycling one fourth of the time and walking the rest. The next day he cycles (at the same speed as before) for half the time and walks the rest (at the same speed as before) and covers 26 km in 2 hours. The speed in km/h at which Budhan walks is
questions.explanation:
We need to determine Budhan's walking speed based on his travel data over two consecutive days. 1. Set Up the Variables
Let the cycling speed be \(C\) km/h and the walking speed be \(W\) km/h. Both days involve a total travel duration of \(2\) hours . 2. Formulate Equations from the Conditions
  • Day 1 Scenario: He cycles for one-fourth of the total time (\(2 \times \dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{1}{2}\) hour) and walks the rest (\(2 - \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{3}{2}\) hours), covering a distance of \(19\) km : \[C\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) + W\left(\frac{3}{2}\right) = 19 \qquad \text{--- (i)}\] Multiplying equation (i) by 2 simplifies it to: \[C + 3W = 38 \qquad \text{--- (iii)}\]
  • Day 2 Scenario: He cycles for half of the total time (\(2 \times \dfrac{1}{2} = 1\) hour) and walks the rest (\(2 - 1 = 1\) hour), covering a distance of \(26\) km : \[C(1) + W(1) = 26 \implies C + W = 26 \qquad \text{--- (ii)}\]
3. Solve the System of Linear Equations
Subtract equation (ii) directly from equation (iii) to eliminate variable \(C\): \[(C + 3W) - (C + W) = 38 - 26\] \[2W = 12\] \[W = 6 \text{ km/h}\] Budhan's walking speed is \(6\) km/h, which corresponds to option (D) . \[\boxed{\text {D) 6}}\]

questions.question:
The points in the graph below represent the halts of a lift for durations of 1 minute, over a period of 1 hour. Which of the following statements are correct?
  1. The elevator never moves directly from any non-ground floor to another non-ground floor over the one hour period
  2. The elevator stays on the fourth floor for the longest duration over the one hour period
questions.explanation:
We need to evaluate two statements based on the elevator halt graph, where each circle represents a 1-minute stop . 1. Evaluate Statement i:
"The elevator never moves directly from any non-ground floor to another non-ground floor..."
  • Look at the time interval between 10 min and 15 min:
  • At \(t = 10\), the lift is on Floor 5.
  • At \(t = 11, 12, 13\), the lift is on Floor 3.
Since it transitioned directly from Floor 5 to Floor 3 without stopping at Floor 0 (ground) in between, the statement is incorrect. \(\implies\) Statement i is FALSE . 2. Evaluate Statement ii:
"The elevator stays on the fourth floor for the longest duration..." Let us count the total number of halt circles (minutes) for the highest-occurring candidate floors:
  • Floor 4 halts: \(3 \text{ (at } 5\text{)} + 4 \text{ (at } 16\text{)} + 3 \text{ (at } 26\text{)} + 2 \text{ (at } 35\text{)} + 3 \text{ (at } 45\text{)} + 2 \text{ (at } 52\text{)} + 2 \text{ (at } 58\text{)} = 19 \text{ minutes}\)
  • Floor 0 halts: Counting the points along the bottom line (\(y = 0\)) quickly reveals more than \(20\) total circles (e.g., long consecutive clusters at 0–3, 7–9, 14–15, 20–22, 29–31, etc.) .
Since Floor 0 has the longest cumulative duration, the statement is incorrect. \(\implies\) Statement ii is FALSE . Since neither statement is correct, the answer matches option D . \[\boxed{\text {D) Neither i nor ii}}\]
